disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type) is characterized by a persistent combination of mood episodes meeting criteria for major depression along with psychotic symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations, with psychotic features present for a substantial portion of the illness and for at least two weeks in the absence of prominent mood symptoms. The depressive component typically involves sustained low mood, loss of interest, and other neurovegetative and cognitive changes, while the psychotic features may be mood-congruent or incongruent. Over time, the course can be episodic or chronic, often leading to functional impairment in work, relationships, and self‑care. It is distinguished from major depressive disorder with psychotic features by the persistence of psychosis outside mood episodes, and from schizophrenia by the prominence and duration of mood symptoms across the illness.

narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, Christina took on a series of high‑end residential contracts while preparing for her contractor licensing exams, working late nights on job sites and then going straight to community theater rehearsals or painting in her home studio. The sustained pressure to grow her business, maintain her reputation for meticulous design work, and stay visible in the local arts scene gradually eroded her sleep schedule and left little time for rest or family life. Over the following months, coworkers and her husband noticed she became increasingly withdrawn on job sites, missed design details she normally prized, and started canceling theater commitments, yet she pushed herself harder to keep contracts from slipping. The condition became clinically significant when she began losing clients due to repeated mistakes and no‑shows, and after a tense meeting where a long‑time builder questioned her reliability, she broke down in front of her pastor, who urged her to see a psychiatrist when she described her internal experiences and how she could no longer trust her own judgment at work.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like there’s something going on behind the scenes on my jobs, like people are plotting around my designs, and no one can convince me otherwise.”

narrative.stressor: Stephen’s difficulties began to take shape as he started seriously planning for retirement from his long‑held janitorial position, when his employer announced a restructuring that would phase out several senior staff roles over the next two years. The prospect of losing his familiar routine, social ties at work, and sense of purpose as the reliable "go‑to" person for younger workers left him increasingly preoccupied with what his days would look like and whether he would be forgotten or discarded. Over the subsequent year and a half, his friends at the anglers club and woodworking class noticed he stopped showing up regularly, let his garden go despite usually being meticulous, and became unusually pessimistic about the point of preparing for the future. He finally agreed to see a mental health professional after his pastor and a supervisor both expressed concern that he was talking more about feeling like his life’s work had been meaningless and that he was too drained to care for himself or his home the way he always had.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m exhausted all the time, like I’m running on empty no matter how much I rest, and I just don’t have the energy to keep up with anything anymore.”

narrative.stressor: Cynthia’s condition became prominent after the unexpected death of her older sister, who had been her closest confidante and partner in church, quilting circles, and community events. In the months after the funeral, she tried to keep up her organizing work, sunrise walks, and gardening, but gradually began canceling commitments, leaving projects unfinished, and spending more time alone at home, telling friends she "just couldn’t feel the joy" in the things they used to share. Over the following year and five months, her church community and neighbors noticed she stopped attending choir, rarely joined birdwatching outings, and seemed unable to take pleasure even in her beloved garden or historical novels, which was a marked change from her usual lively engagement. Concern grew when she openly questioned why she should keep trying, admitted that nothing in her life felt worth doing anymore, and eventually agreed—at her daughter’s insistence and after a tearful conversation with her pastor—to see a psychiatrist because she felt she had "lost all interest in the world" she had worked so hard to nurture.
narrative.chief_complaint: “The things that used to mean everything to me—my garden, my quilts, my walks—don’t matter anymore, and I can’t make myself care about any of it.”
